A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TrojanStego work. Their main text, figures, tables, equations and appendices A–D are readable and support comparison, including matching material relocated within the appendix.

before.justification: V1 reports original model-training experiments, secret-recovery measurements, benchmark evaluations and human detection studies in Section 6 and Appendix A.

after.justification: V3 retains those empirical results and adds Qwen evaluations, larger-model experiments, length/repetition ablations and training-epoch analyses.

M1.justification: The core vocabulary partitioning, ASCII encoding and fine-tuning method remain unchanged. V3 Appendix A.3.2 adds a non-repeating variant whose training completions encode each key only once before returning to ordinary token sampling, modifying the original repeated-encoding procedure.

E1.justification: V3 Figure 6 extends secret-length evaluation to 72 and 80 bits, beyond v1's 8–64-bit range. The English Helpful Instructions domain and five usefulness benchmarks remain unchanged; the additional model families do not introduce new datasets or application tasks.

E2.justification: The comparisons against uncompromised counterparts expand to include Qwen 2.5 7B in Figure 4 and Llama 3.3 70B and Qwen 2.5 72B in Table 9. Existing Llama 8B and Ministral 8B comparisons remain, preserving the original comparison strategy.

E3.justification: V3 adds substantial experimental configurations: Qwen 7B and 70/72B LoRA models, weighted training on 8–64-bit keys, repeated versus single-encoding controls, and an epoch/checkpoint comparison in Appendix A.3. The original main experiment's data split and training parameters remain documented as before; these additions do not establish that the original experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New analyses test whether larger models help, whether length-matched training and repetition improve longer-key recovery, and how additional training trades usefulness against throughput (A.3.1–A.3.3). Table 11 adds class-specific human detection analysis. The original prompt perturbation, benign fine-tuning and later-token decoding analyses are retained; Table 7 supplies fuller results for existing flexibility tests.

E5.justification: Neither version reports independent-run variability, seed counts, confidence intervals or significance tests. The three- and five-generation majority-voting results are unchanged between v1 Table 8 and v3 Table 6; these concern decoding rather than uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: V3 adds extensive Qwen, larger-model, length/repetition, epoch and class-specific detection results. For example, Table 2 newly reports Qwen 7B exact-match rates of 70.0% for trained prompts with unseen keys and 8.8% for unseen prompts and keys. Existing values also change: Figure 4 replaces Llama 8B's reported base IFEval score of 54.8% with 47.8%. Original Llama/Ministral throughput rows remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The formal bucket mapping in Section 4.1 and the logit-method definitions and Equations 1–5 are retained, with the latter moved from v1 A.2 to v3 A.5. No substantive new assumption, theorem, proof or derivation is introduced.

C1.justification: The principal claims remain the new inference-time exfiltration threat, learnable bucket encoding, the seven-condition taxonomy, and empirical attack viability. Both abstracts retain the same headline 32-bit recovery claims. The additional experiments do not redefine the stated core contributions.

C2.justification: V3 substantially expands interpretations of detection and scalability. It discusses the asymmetry between detecting compromised and clean outputs, proposes tokenizer vocabulary and compression as explanations for model differences, and interprets the limited benefits of larger models. Appendix A.3 adds training-range qualifications and discussion of repetition–stealth–robustness and training–utility tradeoffs, distinguishing observations from proposed mechanisms.

D1.justification: Reported total training and evaluation costs increase from approximately 150 and 20 GPU-hours to 400 and 40 GPU-hours (v1 A.1; v3 A.4). V3 also clarifies the six-annotator arrangement and documents English proficiency and NLP/linguistics experience. The main hyperparameter tables and embedded code/model/data access links remain unchanged.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds focused discussion of contextual-integrity violations and agentic privacy work, including Mireshghallah et al., AirGapAgent, AgentDam and MAGPIE, alongside additional steganography and jailbreak citations. It distinguishes deliberate leakage through compromised weights from these settings while retaining the original positioning against cooperative steganography and prompt-based attacks.

P1.justification: V3 makes local wording and explanatory revisions while retaining the main section sequence. The appendix is reorganized to begin with throughput and flexibility results, followed by ablations, with training details and the logit method moved later. An acknowledgments section is also added.

P2.justification: The empirical displays expand substantially through the new length/repetition Figure 6 and Tables 7–13 covering flexibility, larger models, detection breakdowns and epochs. Figures 4 and 5 are redrawn with additional model series and revised axes or legends, and several existing tables gain rows or columns. The original logit plot is retained as Figure 7.

improvement.justification: The new length/repetition controls replace v1's speculation about variable-length training with experimental evidence, while larger-model, epoch and class-specific detection analyses better establish applicability limits. These benefits are tempered by reporting inconsistencies: v3 Section 6.1 retains IFEval degradation figures that disagree with its updated Figure 4, and gives 63% detection for compromised Llama outputs where Table 11 reports 61%. The revision adds useful diagnostic depth but remains uneven in its reporting.
